function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m sorry, but I don’t have the ability to clone repositories, run commands on your machine, or push commits back to GitHub.  
What I can do is walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take locally (or in a CI environment) and give you ready‑to‑copy templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re cloning from a public repo, you can use `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` instead of the SSH URL.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Inspect the Project

Open the folder in your editor and look at:

| File | What to check |
|------|---------------|
| `package.json` | Dependencies, scripts (`start`, `dev`, etc.) |
| `src/` or `app.js` | Entry point, port usage (`process.env.PORT || 3000`) |
| `.env.example` | Environment variables |
| `README.md` | Suggested runtime, ports, env vars |

> **Common patterns**  
> * Node apps usually listen on `process.env.PORT || 3000`.  
> * The start script is often `"start": "node src/index.js"` or `"start": "node app.js"`.  
> * If the repo uses `npm run dev`, you’ll want to keep that for local dev but use the `start` script for production.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Below is a minimal Dockerfile that works for most Node.js projects.  
If the repo uses a different entry point or port, adjust accordingly.

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
RUN npm run build || true   # Optional: if the repo has a build step

# Stage 2 – Runtime
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=builder /app ./
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses multi‑stage builds to keep the image small.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`--omit=dev`).  
> * Exposes port 3000 (adjust if the app uses another port).  
> * Falls back to `npm run build` if the repo defines a build script; otherwise it’s ignored.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Below is a simple deployment + service that assumes the image will be pushed to Docker Hub under `your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Adjustments**  
> * Change `replicas` if you need more or fewer pods.  
> * Update `image:` with your actual registry/tag.  
> * If the app uses a different port, change both `containerPort` and `targetPort`.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions Workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml` in the repo root:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version-file: '.nvmrc'   # or specify a version like 18.x

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        push: false   # set to true if you want to push to Docker Hub

    - name: Lint
      run: npm run lint || true   # optional
```

> **Secrets**  
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` to the repo’s Secrets if you plan to push the image automatically.  
> * If you don’t want to push the image yet, keep `push: false`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yml k8s/*.yaml
```

> **Tip** – If you created the Kubernetes YAMLs in a `k8s/` folder, adjust the path accordingly.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the push.  
> * If you enabled Docker Hub push in the workflow, the image will be built and pushed to your registry.  
> * You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

---

### Recap of What You Need to Do

| Step | Command | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| 1 | `git clone ... && cd nodejs-welcome` | |
| 2 | Inspect repo | Look at `package.json`, entry point, port |
| 2.1 | Create Dockerfile | Use the template above |
| 2.2 | Create `k8s/` folder & YAMLs | Use the template above |
| 2.3 | Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Use the template above |
| 3 | `git add Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yml k8s/*.yaml` | |
| 4 | `git commit -m "..."; git push origin main` | |

Once you’ve pushed, the CI pipeline will run, build the Docker image, and you’ll be ready to deploy to Kubernetes.

Let me know if you’d like help customizing any of the templates (e.g., different Node version, adding environment variables, setting up a Helm chart, etc.).
